title: Vote intention
text:
5 Model: constructs and vote intention
A multinomial logit relates vote intention in wave 5 to the five construct scores measured in the same wave, standardized; no later measure enters as a predictor. “Would not vote” (11 respondents) is merged with “don’t know yet” for estimation, as it is too small for its own equation. This merge, the construct scores and the rule of excluding no respondent are provisional (decision log D4, D6, D22, D27). N = 488; categories: CDU/CSU 109, SPD 49, FDP 23, Greens 73, Left 29, AfD 70, Other party 39, Undecided or would not vote 96.









Predicted probability of each intention when one construct is 1 SD below or above its mean and the other four are at their means. The constructs correlate with each other, so each panel shows an association with the other four held constant. Confidence intervals use the delta method.

title: Vote intention
text:
6 Measurement notes

The open-text answers behind “Other party” are not in the extract, so that category cannot be split.
All five constructs were measured in waves 4 and 5; I model wave 5, the later one.

title: Study E: reproducible construct reports
text: These six reports were built from one pipeline: five constructs and vote intention, from the Study E extract. Every number comes from the coding specification and the data, through one command, Rscript run.R. Where a coding choice needs the scientific lead’s approval, the reports mark it as provisional.

title: Study E: reproducible construct reports
section: How I would work at PPBS
text:
How I would work at PPBS

Why I want this work
I like work whose value shows when someone else reruns it. PPBS holds data from many studies, waves and countries, and those data stay trustworthy only if someone looks after the pipeline week by week. I spent the past year building reproducibility checks for Replication Research, and I want to do that work inside a research programme.


What I bring

Auditing external analyses: For Replication Research I compared how CODECHECK and Meta-Psychology verify papers, and built the journal’s workflow on that basis. I still review for CODECHECK.
Self-auditing pipelines: In my MSc thesis (Bayesian spatiotemporal models in R and INLA, on an HPC cluster), every result is tied to the formula and data that produced it. That validation removed several results I had expected to keep.
Familiarity with survey data: The papers I checked were psychology papers, so I worked through their scale scoring, recoding, missing-data handling and reliability code. I co-authored a replication of Geers and Lassiter (2003).
Transparent learning curve: I have not harmonised items across waves for a survey programme. I would start by learning the PPBS instruments, the way this exercise works through the Study E guide.
Core toolkit: I work in R, Quarto, Git and GitHub Actions. For these reports I used targets, renv, testthat, lavaan, lme4, brms, nnet, marginaleffects and ggplot2, with psych as the reference for my reliability code.



First improvement: one specification per study
The briefing asks for a consistent account of how each source item becomes a processed variable. I would keep that account in one machine-readable specification per study. Here, spec/ stores every item’s wording, waves, valid range, non-answer codes, wording direction and stored direction. One set of tested R functions reads it, checks the raw data and scores it.







Action
Plan




What I would keep
The raw files as received, the NR, CF and NRCF sample labels, the master codebook on Drive, and the existing Quarto templates.


What I would change
Reversals, non-answer codes and wave availability move out of report code into one reviewed, version-controlled specification.


How I would check it
Each report’s items and coding section is generated from the specification, and a checker lists every difference between the specification and the documentation for a person to resolve.


In my first week
Reproduce one published report from fixed inputs, write its specification, rerun the pipeline and log every difference.



The checker has already proved useful here. The guide marks antisci_4 as reverse-coded, but the extract stores it already reversed, and three group authoritarianism items too. Reversing them again would have flipped them back. My build now separates wording direction from stored direction and stops if any item correlates negatively with its scale.



Specification against the item guide: 3 of 140 comparisons differ. Each difference has a decision log entry.

The same direction field would also fix the 2016 system justification plots, where reversed values seem to appear under their original agree and disagree labels.


Second improvement: rebuild only what a correction touches
I use targets, so a changed specification row, function or input reruns only what depends on it. When I refactored the processing code during this exercise, the processed file stayed byte-identical, and the matching checksums show it. Each build writes three records:

validation/provenance.csv: source checksum, specification version, code commit, and a flag for uncommitted code;
validation/manifest.csv: a checksum for every output;
validation/issues.csv: a queue for the reviewer, sorted by severity.

I treat a release as final once a second person has rerun the build and matched the checksums, and the lead has signed off the open decisions (docs/release_record.md). That is the CODECHECK idea applied to a data release.
Once these functions have served two studies, I would turn them into a small internal package. It would build on the tools PPBS already uses (haven, codebook, dataMaid, psych) and add only the PPBS-specific layer.
Two smaller steps would come first. I would run dataMaid after the declared missing codes are set, so its screening report shows only real surprises. I would also write each report’s entry in the format of the website’s data/reports.json, so new reports drop into the existing site.


Decision matrix

Decisions I prepare for the lead

Scoring formulas, collapsing categories, names, panel status, models for new outcomes, publication



The reviewer queue above shows the decisions this build leaves open; the questions behind them are listed at the end of this page.


Survey setup, codebooks and decision records
Before fielding, I would give every item a stable ID, export numeric codes together with their labels, store the wave as embedded data and use one code for “not specified”. Study E shows why: gender, income and vote arrive as German text, and non-answer codes differ by item.
I would compare the Drive master codebook with the specification the same way I compared the guide above, and send each mismatch to the codebook owner. A decision from the weekly meeting or from Slack becomes one decision log entry, one pull request that changes the specification, and one reviewer sign-off.
I would also keep a sample register, one row per study, sample and wave. My build checks it against the respondents present.

text:
How these reports use the PPBS template
I started from the published PPBS construct reports and the archived single-file report, and kept their order of sections. I replaced the optional Quarto starter with one parameterised template; each report still covers its four parts: item map and quality checks, cross-sectional results, longitudinal results, and reproducibility.

Added: reliability for every wave, a factor analysis of the RWA facets, and change over time, since Study E is a panel.
Changed: 95% intervals in place of significance stars, groups under 10 respondents suppressed, and response labels in the scored direction. One template, driven by the specification, serves all five constructs.
Left out: candidate, party identity and likeability items, which Study E does not have; the social class index, whose grouping is a lead decision; and the elastic net. Vote intention has its own report.

9 Measurement notes
